props.title: Commissar

sections.content: **Commissar** (1967) stands as one of the most daring Soviet films ever made, shelved for 20 years due to its unflinching portrayal of a pregnant Red Army commissar during the Russian Civil War. Director Aleksandr Askoldov's only feature film shares DNA with other suppressed masterpieces like **The Color of Pomegranates** (1969) and **Andrei Rublev** (1966), challenging Soviet cinema's established narrative boundaries. The film's stark black-and-white cinematography and expressionistic sequences, particularly the haunting Holocaust premonition, influenced later works like **Come and See** (1985).

sections.content: The film's treatment of Jewish life and identity was revolutionary for Soviet cinema, predating later examinations like Wings (1966) and The Ascent (1977). Askoldov's decision to center the story on a Jewish family, showing their traditions and humanity while hinting at their future fate, broke significant taboos. The film's visual poetry, particularly in domestic scenes, creates a striking contrast with its brutal war sequences, establishing a template that influenced directors like Elem Klimov and Kira Muratova.

The lead performance by Nonna Mordyukova as Commissar Vavilova ranks among the greatest in Soviet cinema, comparable to Tatyana Samoylova in **The Cranes Are Flying** (1957). Her transformation from hardened soldier to expectant mother explores themes of femininity and military duty that wouldn't be addressed again until films like **The Dawns Here Are Quiet** (1972). sections.content: After its release in 1988, **Commissar** became a touchstone for post-Soviet filmmakers dealing with historical trauma. Its influence can be seen in works like **East/West** (1999) and **House of Fools** (2002), which similarly tackle difficult historical subjects through personal stories. The film's unique blend of realism and expressionism created a pathway for directors like Aleksandr Sokurov and his **Russian Ark** (2002).
